item_name: Selective prediction and reject option for safe interventions (SelectiveNet, Geifman and El-Yaniv, conformal risk control)
bibliography: Primary sources. (1) Yonatan Geifman, Ran El-Yaniv (Technion). 'Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks'. NeurIPS (NIPS) 2017. arXiv:1705.08500 (v1 23 May 2017; v2 1 Jun 2017, the current version; https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08500, PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.08500v2). The arXiv page gives no venue; the NeurIPS 2017 publication is from the outline and general knowledge and was not checked on the proceedings page [uncertain]. No code link on the arXiv page. The algorithm is SGR (Selection with Guaranteed Risk). (2) Yonatan Geifman, Ran El-Yaniv. 'SelectiveNet: A Deep Neural Network with an Integrated Reject Option'. ICML 2019 (PMLR 97). arXiv:1901.09192 (v1 26 Jan 2019 ... v4 26 Jun 2019, the current version; the arXiv comment says 'Accepted to ICML 2019'). 'Conformal Risk Control'. arXiv:2208.02814 (v1 4 Aug 2022; v2 23 Apr 2023; v3 29 Apr 2023; v4 13 Jun 2025, the current version, which was read). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2208.02814. full_text_checked: Read in full from arXiv PDF text: Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017 (v2, all sections, Tables 1-6, Algorithm 1, Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2); SelectiveNet (v4, Sections 1-9, Tables 1-6; the reference list was skimmed); Conformal Risk Control (v4, Sections 1-5, Theorems 1-2, Propositions 1-7, Figures 1-4; Appendix A on the non-monotone asymptotic algorithm and Appendix B proofs were not read in detail). Abstract or search-result level only: RCPS, Learn-then-Test, Feng et al. 2023, Jaeger et al. 2023, Dunn et al. 2023, Lee et al. 2023, Andéol et al. 2023/2025, Li et al. 2022 (PAC MOT), MOT-CUP, Timans et al. 2024. Not opened: the code repositories (geifmany/SelectiveNet, aangelopoulos/conformal-risk, fd-shifts) and the NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR proceedings pages. For the project link, the project file runs/z13_candidates_20261016/report.json (key stats/*) was read to locate the '7 of 37' figure.
task_and_output: Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017 (SGR) take an already trained classifier f and a confidence-rate function kappa (softmax response SR, or minus MC-dropout variance). The output is a selection function g_theta(x) = 1[kappa(x) >= theta] plus a risk bound b*. The threshold theta is chosen by binary search over sorted calibration scores so that the selective 0/1 risk (error among accepted samples) is <= target r* with probability >= 1 - delta. Coverage is maximised subject to this. SelectiveNet (2019) trains one network with three heads: prediction f, selection g (a single sigmoid neuron), and auxiliary h. At inference it predicts iff g(x) >= 0.5, or g(x) >= tau after post-hoc coverage calibration. It handles classification (CIFAR-10, SVHN, Cats vs Dogs) and regression (Concrete, MSE). Conformal Risk Control (CRC) post-processes any model output into a nested family C_lambda (sets, masks, thresholds) and picks lambda_hat so that the EXPECTED loss on a new exchangeable point is <= alpha. The loss must be bounded by B and non-increasing in lambda. Examples are FNR in polyp segmentation, FNR in COCO multilabel classification, hierarchical graph distance on ImageNet and token F1 in open-domain QA. None of the three outputs a bounding box or track. In the applications (Andéol 2023; Li 2022) the outputs are inflated box sets or edge-transition sets.
data_and_independent_videos: SGR: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The standard 10k validation set is randomly split in half, about 5000 calibration and 5000 test. ImageNet ILSVRC validation is split into about 25,000 + 25,000. All are i.i.d. still images with no videos. SelectiveNet: CIFAR-10, SVHN, Cats vs Dogs (25,000 images, 64x64) and UCI Concrete Compressive Strength (tabular). Standard train/test splits; coverage calibration uses an independent unlabeled validation set V_n (size not stated in the text read). CRC: polyp segmentation pooled from Kvasir, Hyper-Kvasir, CVC-ColonDB, CVC-ClinicDB and ETIS-Larib, with n = 1000 calibration and 781 evaluation. MS COCO, n = 4000 / 1000. ImageNet hierarchical, n = 30,000 / 20,000. Natural Questions, n = 2500 / 1110. Every experiment uses 1000 random calibration/evaluation re-splits of i.i.d. items. No experiment in the three primary papers uses video, and none splits by independent sequences. Applications: Li et al. 2022 evaluate on MOT-17 (7 training sequences publicly labelled); how they split calibration from test was not checked [uncertain]. Andéol 2023 use a new railway dataset of images from the train driver's viewpoint; whether calibration and test are split by sequence was not stated in the abstract [uncertain].
target_size_and_input_resolution: Not applicable to the selection mechanism itself. Inputs are CIFAR/SVHN 32x32, Cats vs Dogs 64x64, ImageNet at standard VGG-16/ResNet-50 resolution, segmentation d x d images and COCO images at TResNet resolution. No target-size analysis. The methods are agnostic to resolution because they act on a scalar score or a set-valued output.
frame_rate_and_camera_motion: Not applicable. All primary experiments use independent still images or text. There is no temporal sampling, camera motion or sequential dependence. The guarantees assume exchangeable (SGR: i.i.d.) samples, which consecutive frames or interventions from one video are not.
detector_and_exemplar: No detector and no exemplar in the primary works. The selector acts on a pre-trained classifier's score (SGR, CRC) or a jointly trained selection head (SelectiveNet). In the detection applications (Andéol 2023, Li 2022, Timans 2024) the detector is fixed and pre-trained, and conformal calibration only post-processes its boxes. There is no exemplar-conditioned re-identification.
trainable_nodes_and_loss: SGR: nothing trained. One scalar threshold theta is fitted by binary search over ceil(log2 m) candidates. Each candidate's bound comes from the exact binomial tail (Gascuel and Caraux 1992, Lemma 3.1) at confidence delta/ceil(log2 m), with a union bound. SelectiveNet: the full network is trained with L = alpha*L_(f,g) + (1 - alpha)*L_h. L_(f,g) = empirical selective risk + lambda*max(0, c - empirical coverage)^2, an interior-point-style quadratic penalty with target coverage c. L_h is the ordinary loss of an auxiliary head on all samples. alpha = 0.5 and lambda = 32 in all experiments (Sec. 4.2, 6.3). The selection head on VGG-16 is FC 512 + BN + ReLU + FC 1 + sigmoid. For regression it has one hidden layer of 16 ReLU units. The paper says the auxiliary head is essential: without it the network 'will focus on a fraction c of the training set' and overfit the wrong subset. Exact parameter counts are not given. CRC: nothing trained. A single scalar lambda_hat = inf{lambda : n/(n+1) * R_hat_n(lambda) + B/(n+1) <= alpha}, with lambda_max if the set is empty (Eq. 4).
controls_seeds_splits: SGR: SR versus MC-dropout confidence functions as controls. One calibration/test split per dataset (random halves). delta = 0.001, with no Bonferroni correction across the 6-7 target risks in each table (footnote 2). No repeated seeds. SelectiveNet: baselines are SR and MC-dropout (p = 0.5, 100 passes for classification; p = 0.05, 200 passes for regression) on the same main body. Results are mean +/- std. The text says 'Each selective risk in the table is an average over three independent runs' for Table 6, and similar repetition is implied for Tables 1-5 [uncertain]. A train-coverage x calibration-coverage matrix (Table 6) controls for the calibration step. CRC: 1000 random calibration/evaluation splits per task. No baseline method is compared; the experiments only check validity (mean risk <= alpha) and set size. Later critiques (Feng et al. 2023; Jaeger et al. 2023) act as external controls. They report that SelectiveNet-style heads do not beat softmax response on a classifier trained equally well, and that SR is the strongest overall failure detector, including under shift (abstract level).
metrics_and_numbers: SGR (arXiv 1705.08500v2), all at delta = 0.001. CIFAR-10 (Table 1): r* = 0.01 gives test risk 0.0092 at test coverage 0.7856, bound 0.0099. r* = 0.02 gives 0.0149 / 0.8466 / 0.0199. r* = 0.06 gives 0.0572 / 0.9784 / 0.0600. CIFAR-100 (Table 2): r* = 0.02 gives 0.0187 / 0.2134 / 0.0197. r* = 0.10 gives 0.0938 / 0.5952 / 0.0998. r* = 0.25 gives 0.2395 / 0.8826 / 0.2499. ImageNet VGG-16 top-1 (Table 3): r* = 0.02 gives 0.0131 / 0.2322. r* = 0.10 gives 0.0948 / 0.5951. ImageNet VGG-16 top-5 (Table 4): r* = 0.02 gives 0.0179 / 0.5351. ResNet-50 top-5 (Table 6): r* = 0.02 gives 0.0189 / 0.5935 / 0.0200. This last row is the abstract's '2% top-5 error with almost 60% coverage'. In every table the test risk stays below the bound b*. Sec. 5, Fig. 2c: on ImageNet top-1 at 60% coverage, SR has about 10% error versus more than 20% for MC-dropout. SelectiveNet (arXiv 1901.09192v4). Table 1, CIFAR-10 realised test coverage for target c: SR 60.19 vs SelectiveNet 77.34 at c = 0.70, and 82.30 vs 90.99 at c = 0.95. Average violation is 11.98 (SR) vs 3.63 (SelectiveNet) percentage points before calibration. Sec. 5: after calibration, tau = 100(1 - c) percentile of g on V_n, with Hoeffding coverage error eps = sqrt(ln(2/delta)/(2n)). The printed bound '2e^{2n eps^2}' is missing the minus sign. Table 2, CIFAR-10 selective error (%): coverage 0.70 gives 0.32 +/- 0.01 (SelectiveNet), 0.43 (MC-dropout), 0.42 (SR). Coverage 0.95 gives 4.16 vs 4.58 vs 4.55. Coverage 1.00 gives 6.79 for all. Table 4, Cats vs Dogs at 0.80: 0.35 vs 0.55 (MCD) vs 0.68 (SR). Table 5, Concrete MSE at 0.70: 27.94 vs 33.70 (MCD). Table 6: calibrating to a coverage far from the trained c costs risk; e.g. model trained at c = 0.70 and calibrated to 0.90 gives 2.65 vs 2.43 for the model trained at c = 0.90. CRC (arXiv 2208.02814v4). Theorem 1: E[L_{n+1}(lambda_hat)] <= alpha under exchangeability, non-increasing right-continuous L_i, L_i(lambda_max) <= alpha and L_i <= B. Theorem 2: if additionally i.i.d., L_i >= 0 and no jumps at fixed lambda, then E[L] >= alpha - 2B/(n+1). Proposition 1: for non-monotone losses the risk can reach B - eps, i.e. no control. Corollary 1 restores control by monotonising, but this is powerful only when the loss is nearly monotone. Sec. 3, risk over 1000 splits: polyp FNR at alpha = 0.1, mean 0.0987, sd 0.0114. COCO FNR at alpha = 0.1, mean 0.0996, sd 0.0052. ImageNet graph distance at alpha = 0.05, mean 0.0499, sd 0.0011. NQ F1 at alpha = 0.3, mean 0.2996, sd 0.0150. Sec. 4.1, shift: with a known bounded likelihood ratio w, apply CRC to w*L. Covariate shift with a known w(x) allows unbounded w (Proposition 2). For arbitrary shift (Proposition 3), E[L] <= alpha + B * sum_i TV(Z_i, Z_{n+1}). Sec. 4.2, quantile risk control: Quantile_beta(L) <= alpha via indicator losses (Proposition 4). Sec. 4.3, multiple risks: lambda_hat = sup over gamma (Proposition 5). Derived for this project (not in the sources; scipy calculation by this agent): the finite-sample slack B/(n+1) is 0.037 for n = 26, 0.028 for n = 35, 0.013 for n = 75 and 0.0095 for n = 104 independent videos. With zero observed failures among k accepted calibration items, a one-sided bound of risk <= r* at confidence 1 - delta needs k >= ln(1/delta)/r*: k >= 30 for r* = 0.1 and delta = 0.05, k >= 15 for r* = 0.2. Hoeffding coverage error at delta = 0.05 is 0.0149 for n = 8326 items, 0.148 for n = 84 and 0.223 for n = 37. Project number for comparison: runs/z13_candidates_20261016/report.json, key stats/D_base, gives top1_tau 0.9477, selected_known 37, selected_unknown 47 and selected_known_bad_fraction 0.8108. That is 7 useful out of 37 known, or 7 out of 84 selected (8.3%). The Clopper-Pearson 95% interval for 7/37 useful is [0.080, 0.352].
tested_conditions: Unseen videos: no. None of the primary papers uses video; the test items are unseen i.i.d. images. Target absence: not reported as such. Rejection is generic and can encode 'no valid answer', but no experiment has an explicit 'object absent' class. Similar distractors: not reported. Occlusion: not reported. Night or low light: not reported. Distribution shift: SGR and SelectiveNet do not test it. CRC gives theory (weighted CRC; total-variation degradation, Proposition 3) but no shifted-data experiment. Jaeger et al. 2023 benchmark failure detection under several shifts (abstract level only). Sequential operation on own predictions: no. All guarantees are for one-shot decisions on exchangeable points. Andéol and Masséna 2025 ('Sequential CRC') address a sequential setting, but its details were not read [uncertain]. Li et al. 2022 report PAC sets for tracking edges on MOT-17, but whether the tracker runs on its own corrected outputs was not checked [uncertain].
mechanism_summary: Published mechanisms. (a) SGR. Rank the calibration samples by an existing confidence score. For each candidate threshold, compute the exact binomial upper confidence bound on the error rate among the accepted samples. Pick the lowest threshold whose bound is below the target risk. This gives a high-probability guarantee on precision among accepted items. It does not improve the ranking: if the score ranks poorly, coverage collapses ('if kappa is severely skewed ... the bound ... can be far from the target risk', Sec. 4 footnote). (b) SelectiveNet. Train a separate selection head jointly with the predictor, under a coverage penalty and with an auxiliary full-coverage head that keeps the features general. The selector is supposed to learn where the predictor is reliable. Post-hoc, re-set tau on held-out data so the realised coverage matches the target. Later work (Feng et al. 2023) attributes most of the gain to better predictor training rather than the selection head. (c) CRC. For any loss that falls monotonically as the procedure becomes more conservative, choose the least conservative lambda whose inflated empirical risk n/(n+1)*R_hat + B/(n+1) is <= alpha. This gives an in-expectation (marginal) guarantee over exchangeable calibration and test units. The guarantee is tight to O(1/n), degrades by B times the total-variation distance under shift, and fails for non-monotone losses. Proposed modification for this project (not published). Treat 'apply the FlyVis correction' as the conservative-to-permissive dial lambda = 1 - tau. Make the exchangeable unit a whole video, not an intervention. Define a bounded per-video loss that is monotone in tau, e.g. the number of harmful corrections accepted divided by the number of loss events in that video. Choose tau on calibration videos by CRC or, for a high-probability statement, by an SGR or Learn-then-Test binomial bound, and test once on held-out videos. This only sets tau and certifies a harm rate. It cannot make a weak score useful.
transfer_limits: 1) Exchangeability unit. Interventions within a video share the track, scene, illumination and detector errors, so they are not exchangeable. A valid guarantee needs videos (or hierarchical units, Dunn et al. 2023; Lee et al. 2023) as the calibration unit. Our calibration pools are train26 (26 videos) and dev35 (35), with train104 for fitting and heldout75 for a single final test. With n = 26 or 35 the CRC slack B/(n+1) is 0.037 or 0.028 of the loss range, and Theorem 2's tightness slack 2B/(n+1) is 0.074 or 0.056. Small but not negligible for rare-event losses. 2) Rare events. The FlyVis correction is meant for a small top fraction (the 1% tier gave 84 selected interventions in runs/z13_candidates_20261016/report.json, stats/D_base). An SGR-style bound on harm among accepted items has very few labelled positives. With 37 known outcomes of which 30 were harmful (bad fraction 0.811), the 95% Clopper-Pearson lower bound on the harmful fraction is about 0.65 (1 - 0.352). No threshold at this tier can be certified as mostly useful. The procedure would correctly return 'abstain everywhere', i.e. zero coverage. 3) Unknown labels. 47 of 84 selected interventions have unknown usefulness (no annotated frame). CRC and SGR need the loss on every calibration unit. Dropping unknowns biases the result if missingness depends on conditions (night, occlusion). The conservative option is to score unknowns as worst case B, which with 56% unknown makes any useful alpha unreachable. 4) Monotonicity. Conditional selective risk (harm among accepted) is a ratio and is not monotone in tau in finite samples, so CRC Theorem 1 does not apply to it directly. Use either a per-opportunity harm loss (monotone: raising tau accepts fewer) or the SGR/LTT high-probability route for the ratio. A ΔHOTA-per-video loss is generally non-monotone in tau because track interactions are combinatorial. Proposition 1 then voids the guarantee unless the loss is monotonised (Corollary 1), which loses power. 5) Shift. Day/night, weather and camera differences between dev35/train26 and heldout75 or val break exchangeability. Proposition 3 adds B * sum TV, which is uninformative for large shifts. Weighted CRC needs a known or estimated likelihood ratio and labelled-domain overlap. Conditioning on night as a separate calibration stratum halves n again. 6) Guarantee type. CRC controls the expected loss, i.e. the average harm across future videos, not the worst video. The quantile version (Proposition 4) or RCPS/LTT is needed for 'harm <= alpha in at least 90% of videos', and these need more units. 7) No ranking improvement. All post-hoc methods (SGR, CRC, SelectiveNet's tau calibration) only move the operating point along an existing risk-coverage curve. Our problem is that the curve itself is poor (top-1% precision about 19% among known). 8) SelectiveNet's joint head applies to a FlyVis readout, but the external evidence (Feng 2023, Jaeger 2023) says a separate head rarely beats a well-trained predictor's own score. Our setting already has a learned presence score that fails. 9) Our environment: YOLO/ByteTrack/MASA decide association after the correction, so a 'useful' correction at the centre level may still not change HOTA. The loss must be defined on the tracker-level effect, which makes it noisy and possibly non-monotone. Identity among similar neighbours is not modelled by any of these sources.
research_questions_addressed: Q4 (main): direct methodological evidence on how to set tau with a guarantee and what it needs. SGR/LTT certify precision among accepted items with a high-probability binomial bound. CRC certifies expected per-unit harm. SelectiveNet shows joint training of predictor and selector with a coverage target. The caution is that none of these improves a weak ranking, and the critiques (Feng 2023, Jaeger 2023) show that dedicated selection heads seldom beat the predictor's own score once the predictor is trained well. This argues for improving the localisation-quality signal inside the FlyVis readout, not adding an external head. The answer to Q4's 'answer changes if' condition is no: these sources contain no direct result where a separate quality head improves intervention selection under distribution shift. Q5 (secondary): sets the minimum statistical budget. A CRC or SGR check on train26/dev35 is cheap (CPU only, no GPU). With n = 26-35 videos and about 7-37 labelled accepted events per tier, it can only certify loose bounds. It also gives a clean stop condition: if the binomial lower bound on harm at every tau exceeds the tolerated rate, stop the intervention line at that tier. Q2 (caution only): the risk-coverage curve and AURC give a readout-independent way to compare B/C/D selection quality on identical observations. They separate 'score ranks badly' from 'threshold set badly', but not representation from readout. Q1 and Q3: not addressed.
candidate_node_change: Node: readout (refusal output of the FlyVis object readout), plus protocol for tau. This is an analogy from SelectiveNet, not a published FlyVis result. Change: train the readout's refusal or quality output jointly with the centre correction under a coverage-constrained selective loss, L = 0.5*[selective localisation loss on accepted + lambda*max(0, c - coverage)^2] + 0.5*[full-coverage auxiliary localisation loss], with c set to the intended intervention rate (e.g. 0.01-0.05). The quality target is 'correction moves the centre closer to the annotated target than the stock prediction'. This replaces the current presence probability. The core and the input stay as in D, so the change stays inside the FlyVis readout node. Controls, all on identical train104 observations and histories: (1) stand without correction; (2) B, the same readout and selective loss with no FlyVis (~9602-parameter network); (3) C, frozen stock FlyVis with the same readout; (4) D, trained FlyVis with the same readout. A FlyVis result exists only if D (or C) beats B at equal coverage. tau protocol: fit on train104. Calibrate tau on train26 with the video as the unit, using (a) SGR/Clopper-Pearson for 'harmful fraction among accepted <= r*' at delta = 0.1, and (b) CRC for per-video harm rate <= alpha with unknown-outcome events scored as B = 1. Freeze tau before dev35. Then one MASA HOTA comparison on dev35 per the established protocol, with heldout75 untouched until a single final run. Minimal check (CPU, cheap): risk-coverage curves and AURC for B/C/D at coverages 0.5%, 1%, 2% and 5% on train26 known outcomes, with a video-level bootstrap. First, compute whether the existing presence score can certify any tier. From the current numbers it cannot (7/37 useful; lower bound on harm about 0.65). Stop conditions, written before the run: (i) if the retrained selector's useful fraction among known at the 1% tier is not above that of B by a video-bootstrap CI excluding 0, stop. The gain would not be attributable to FlyVis. (ii) If no tau on train26 gives a one-sided 90% upper bound on harmful fraction below 0.5 with at least 15 known accepted events, do not run HOTA. Record 'abstain is the certified policy'. (iii) If the dev35 realised harmful fraction exceeds the train26 bound, report a shift violation and stop tuning; do not re-fit tau on dev35.
strongest_objection: These methods choose an operating point on an existing risk-coverage curve and certify it under exchangeability. Our bottleneck is the curve itself: at the 1% tier only 7 of 37 known corrections were useful, and 47 of 84 had unknown outcomes (runs/z13_candidates_20261016/report.json, stats/D_base). Any honest calibration will therefore certify 'abstain', which is safe but adds nothing to HOTA. The guarantees also need video-level exchangeability between calibration and deployment, which day/night and weather shifts break. With only 26-35 calibration videos and a few dozen labelled events, the bounds are loose. SelectiveNet-style joint selection heads, the only constructive part, have been shown (Feng et al. 2023; Jaeger et al. 2023) to give little beyond a well-trained predictor's own score, so they are not strong evidence that a FlyVis quality head would rank better.
evidence_strength: Strong for the mathematical guarantees and their assumptions. All three primary works are peer-reviewed (NeurIPS 2017; ICML 2019; CRC at ICLR 2024 [uncertain]), the proofs are in the text, CRC and SelectiveNet code is public (repositories not opened), and the conformal guarantees are widely replicated in follow-up work. Moderate to weak as evidence for our decision. There are no video, tracking or shift experiments in the primary papers. Detection/tracking applications (Andéol 2023 COPA; PAC-MOT 2022 preprint; MOT-CUP preprint) were checked only at abstract level. Independent critiques weaken SelectiveNet's specific claim that a separate selection head adds value. Overall: strong for 'how to set and certify tau'; weak for 'this will make FlyVis interventions useful'.
